A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same mCLM research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices support reliable comparison, including matching relocated sections and figures.

before.justification: v2 reports original FDA-drug property-editing experiments, synthesizability evaluations, ADMET oracle results, and iterative molecule-editing case studies.

after.justification: v3 retains those original empirical results and adds HierVAE and DGAE comparisons, QM9 synthesizability results, and component and backbone ablations.

M1.justification: The proposed tokenization pipeline, GNN and adapter architecture, Qwen backbone, training objectives, and iterative editing procedure remain unchanged. Appendix F adds reconstruction documentation; the alternative encoders, tokenizer, and backbone are experimental ablations rather than revisions to the proposed method.

E1.justification: Appendix H adds a QM9-based generation and synthesizability evaluation, extending the evaluated molecular population beyond FDA-drug editing. QM9 was already a training-data source in Appendix G. The existing ADMET tasks, FDA evaluations, and fallen-angel cases remain.

E2.justification: v3 adds two substantively different comparator families: HierVAE for property optimization and synthesizability in Tables 8–9, and vector-quantized DGAE for QM9 synthesizability in Table 10. The seven existing molecular-editing baselines remain, substantially broadening the comparison beyond the previous comparator set.

E3.justification: New experiments specify property-specific HierVAE training, an existing QM9-trained DGAE checkpoint, synthesis-guaranteed QM9 blocks for mCLM, and representation and 3B-backbone controls. These extend the experimental settings; the existing FDA evaluation sizes, TDC splits, metrics, and stated Allchemy search protocol remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix I introduces direct tests of the GNN encoder, synthesis-aware tokenization through substitution with BRICS blocks, and Qwen versus Llama backbones. Tables 2 and 11 report their synthesizability and property-editing effects, with validation-loss evidence for the backbone comparison. Existing case studies and token-neighbor analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report point estimates without repeated-run counts, random-seed reporting, confidence intervals, error bars, or formal significance tests. The additional results follow the existing reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 8–11 add substantial results: HierVAE reports 10.5% average property improvement versus mCLM's retained 15.0%, and the new QM9 comparison reports 62% versus 100% synthesizability for DGAE and mCLM. HierVAE achieves better SA but lower retrosynthetic synthesizability than mCLM. New ablation outcomes are also reported. Existing table values remain; separately, Section 3.2 changes MoleculeSTM makeability from 85.4% to 84.8%, conflicting with the unchanged 85.39% in Table 2.

T1.justification: The mathematical loss formulation and Appendix A.1 derivation of 2n−3 synthesis steps are retained. Appendix F's added reconstruction example explains implementation rather than introducing a formal definition, theorem, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal introduction and conclusion claims retain the same scope: synthesis-compatible modular tokens, joint chemical-language modeling, property improvement, unseen-block generalization, and iterative editing. The additional experiments support these retained claims rather than redefine the contribution.

C2.justification: Appendix H adds substantive interpretations of HierVAE's performance, possible benefits from mCLM-preprocessed training molecules, and disagreement between SA and retrosynthesis scores. It newly acknowledges restricted Allchemy discrimination on the FDA distribution. Appendix I interprets the Llama results as possible overfitting. The earlier multi-objective optimization caveat remains.

D1.justification: v3 adds front-page data/model and code links where v2 promised future release. Appendix F documents connection-point placeholders, their GNN encoding, and worked imatinib reconstruction steps. These improve access instructions and implementation disclosure; the existing core training recipe remains unchanged.

R1.justification: Section 4 and Appendix H substantially expand positioning against closely relevant alternatives, including SAFE, Group-SELFIES, Reasyn, discrete molecular representations, DGAE, and HierVAE. They distinguish synthesis-compatible blocks from line representations and learned codebooks, extending the earlier, more general discussion of atom- and fragment-based approaches.

P1.justification: Most existing prose remains intact. v3 adds focused explanations, corrects wording, swaps the library-design and fallen-angel subsections, removes the A.1.1 subheading while retaining its text, and appends baseline and ablation sections and acknowledgments. This is a limited reorganization rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: The experimental displays expand with dedicated baseline, QM9, and ablation tables in Tables 8–11, while Table 2 gains ablation rows and a clearer caption. Figure 3 is redrawn with numbered connection points. Figures 4–5 exchange order, and the retained token-example figures are repaginated.

improvement.justification: v2 lacked direct tests of its central GNN/tokenizer choices and comparisons with hierarchical and vector-quantized generators. v3 supplies these evaluations, substantially strengthening scrutiny of the main contribution and exposing meaningful tradeoffs. Reconstruction details and discussion of evaluation limits also improve the paper. Differing baseline constraints, absent uncertainty estimates, and the new prose/Table 2 inconsistency temper the evidence, but the gains from addressing these important evaluation gaps are substantial.
